title: Session 3.1: Sources of Innovation — Tech-Push vs. Market-Pull
description: Trace where an innovation's original push came from, and defend that classification with evidence before applying it to your own project.
congratsText: You mastered Sources of Innovation — Tech-Push vs. Market-Pull!

sections.title: Objectives
sections.lesson:
Objectives
  • Tell tech-push and market-pull apart using one deciding question
  • Defend a source classification with dated evidence, not opinion
  • Name the dominant force when an innovation is hybrid

sections.title: Where Solutions Come From
sections.lesson:
Where Solutions Come From
Every solution you will ever evaluate started with a push from somewhere. Sometimes a laboratory built a capability and then went looking for someone who needed it. Sometimes people had been complaining about a problem for years and technology finally arrived to answer them.
That difference is the source of the innovation, and it is the first of three lenses you will use in Chapter 3.
Why the source matters before you judge anything else:
  • It tells you whether the need is already proven or still has to be proven
  • It tells you where the adoption risk sits — in the technology, or in the market
  • It tells you what evidence a reader will demand from your team
A solution with no identifiable demand behind it is not automatically a bad idea. It is an idea carrying a heavier burden of proof, and you need to know that before you commit a semester to it.

quiz.question: Why does identifying an innovation's source matter before you evaluate it?
options: It reveals whether a real need already exists or must be created
It determines whether the technology is patented or free to use
It shows how much the original development of the technology cost
It establishes which company currently holds the largest market share

sections.title: Tech-Push
sections.lesson:
Tech-Push
In a tech-push innovation, the capability comes first. Someone invents, discovers, or perfects something — and only afterwards does anyone ask what it is good for.
Two classics:
  • Post-it Notes — 3M produced an adhesive that was too weak to be useful. The product came years later, when someone needed a bookmark that would not fall out of a hymn book.
  • Penicillin — a contaminated dish killed the bacteria around it. Nobody had ordered a mould-based antibiotic; the observation arrived first, the application followed.
What tech-push means for a feasibility study: the technology is usually the safe part, because it demonstrably works. The risk sits on the demand side. Your team has to show that somebody actually wants this, because no queue of complaining customers created it.

quiz.question: A university lab perfects a new battery chemistry, then spends two years looking for an industry that could use it. How is this classified?
options: Tech-push, because the capability existed before any named need
Market-pull, because longer battery life is a standing complaint
Neither, because laboratory research sits outside both categories
Both equally, because all hardware innovation is hybrid by default

sections.title: Market-Pull
sections.lesson:
Market-Pull
In a market-pull innovation, the problem comes first. People were already struggling, already improvising workarounds, already paying too much — and technology showed up to serve a demand that was waiting for it.
Two you already know:
  • Smartphones — people carried a phone, a camera, a music player and a planner. The demand for one device to replace four predates the device by years.
  • GCash — millions of Filipinos had no bank account and were sending money through remittance counters and bus conductors. The pain existed long before the app.
What market-pull means for a feasibility study: demand is the easy part to prove. The hard part is that a visible, painful, documented problem attracts competitors. If the pull is real, somebody is already pulling — which is exactly what your Chapter 4 scan will find.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest evidence that an innovation is market-pull?
options: Documented complaints about the problem predate the technology
The technology behind it was expensive and difficult to develop
Several large companies launched similar products in the same year
The founders describe their product as solving a real user need

sections.title: The Deciding Question
sections.lesson:
The Deciding Question
When a case is genuinely unclear, one question settles it:
What problem existed BEFORE this technology was built?
You can name it
You can point to the problem, say roughly when it started, and cite who complained. The technology arrived into an existing gap. Market-pull.
You cannot name it
The honest answer is that people found uses for it afterwards. The capability arrived first and the applications were assembled around it. Tech-push.
The trap to avoid: "our idea uses technology, so it must be tech-push." Every innovation in this course involves technology. The label is not about whether technology is present — it is about sequence. Which came first, the capability or the complaint?

quiz.question: A team argues "our idea uses AI, so it is tech-push." What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: The presence of technology says nothing about which came first
AI systems are always classified as market-pull in modern practice
Tech-push applies only to hardware, never to software systems
The correct label depends on the size of the market being served

sections.title: Case Files — Market-Pull
sections.lesson:
Case Files — Market-Pull
Apply the deciding question to two familiar cases.
YouTube (2005). Before it launched, people already owned video files — from camcorders, phones and TV clips — and had no way to share them. Email attachments were too large, and personal hosting was too technical for most people. The problem is nameable and dateable. Market-pull.
Grab and Uber. Before either existed, riders were refused by taxis, overcharged off the meter, and left waiting late at night with no record of who picked them up. That complaint is decades older than the smartphone. Market-pull.
Notice what makes both classifications defensible: not that the platforms are popular or profitable, but that the problem is documented earlier than the solution. That is the shape of evidence Chapter 3 expects.

quiz.question: What makes YouTube a market-pull case rather than a tech-push one?
options: People were already failing to share video files before it launched
Flash video streaming was newly invented technology at the time
It grew faster than every competing video platform of its era
Its founders came from engineering rather than from media backgrounds

sections.title: Case Files — Tech-Push
sections.lesson:
Case Files — Tech-Push
Now two cases that fail the deciding question.
Machine learning and AI. The research is decades old. What changed recently was capability — cheap parallel computing and enormous datasets made existing methods work. Only then did industries start asking what they could point it at. Nobody was queuing up demanding neural networks. Tech-push.
Blockchain. A distributed ledger design was published in 2008, and the decade that followed was a public search for applications — supply chains, land titles, certificates, voting. Many of those pilots were quietly abandoned. Tech-push.
The lesson underneath both: a tech-push idea is not disqualified. It simply carries an extra obligation — your team must supply the demand evidence that history did not supply for you. If you cannot, that finding belongs in your study, and a well-evidenced No is a full-marks answer.

quiz.question: Why is blockchain treated as a tech-push case?
options: The capability came first and applications were sought afterwards
It failed to attract serious investment during its first decade
It was created inside an academic laboratory rather than a company
It answers a problem customers had been complaining about for years

sections.title: Hybrids — When Both Forces Act
sections.lesson:
Hybrids — When Both Forces Act
Most real innovations are hybrid. Pure cases are teaching examples; the world is messier.
The smartphone, honestly described:
The pull
People wanted to stop carrying four devices. That demand was documented years before the product shipped.
The push
Capacitive touchscreens, mobile processors and battery density matured on their own schedule, not on the market's.
GCash reads the same way — a genuine pull from unbanked Filipinos, meeting a push from telecom infrastructure that already existed for other reasons.
How to write a hybrid in Chapter 3: answering "both" and stopping is not a classification. Name the dominant force, defend it with dated evidence, then acknowledge the secondary force in one sentence. A reader must be able to see which way you decided and why.

quiz.question: Your team concludes its idea is hybrid. What does Chapter 3 still require?
options: Name the dominant force and support it with dated evidence
Pick one label and remove the evidence for the other side
Cite a published academic source that uses the same label
Explain why hybrid innovations are more common than pure ones

sections.title: Classifying Your Own Project
sections.lesson:
Classifying Your Own Project
In Worksheet 3 you apply this to your own team's idea — so be precise about what you are classifying.
Remember the non-invention rule: nothing may be proposed that does not already exist somewhere in the world. You are not classifying an invention of your own. You are classifying the existing solution your team intends to adopt or adapt.
What a full-marks answer looks like:
  • A named, real, existing solution — not a category or a wish
  • A stated label — tech-push, market-pull, or hybrid with a dominant force
  • Evidence with dates, showing which came first: the capability or the complaint
  • One sentence on what the label implies for adoption risk in your own setting
Source is only the first of the three axes on Worksheet 3. Next session adds Type — disruptive or incremental — and Pattern — improvement, application or recombination. Source tells you where the idea came from; those two tell you how risky it is.

quiz.question: Under the non-invention rule, whose source does your team classify in Chapter 3?
options: The existing solution the team plans to adopt or adapt
The original problem the team documented in Chapter 1
The newest technology mentioned anywhere in the scan
The competitor holding the largest share of the local market

sections.title: Recap
sections.lesson:
Recap
  • Where solutions come from — the source tells you whether the risk sits in the technology or in the market.
  • Tech-push — capability first, application later; the demand still has to be proven.
  • Market-pull — documented problem first; demand is easy to prove, competitors are already there.
  • The deciding question — what problem existed BEFORE this technology was built?
  • Market-pull cases — YouTube and Grab qualify because the complaint is older than the solution.
  • Tech-push cases — ML/AI and blockchain qualify because applications were hunted for afterwards.
  • Hybrids — most innovations are both; name the dominant force instead of stopping at "both".
  • Your own project — classify the real existing solution you will adopt, with dated evidence.
